{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Alex's idea (who:alex), for his work project, relayed by Anthony in the dev_reflow2 hub session on 2026-09-26:

"I am sort of wondering for work though if I could move it to an ec2 instance and expose it and then add it to the mcp list in my project so coworkers don't need to install reflow2."

Anthony's reading: Alex does not much like the local client (option #2, `reflow2-mcp --remote`), so this is his way of making the direct connection (option #1) work for a team — the same shape as flo2's api.flo2.io, but on the company's own machine.

THE IDEA: one reflow2 on an EC2 instance, `reflow2-mcp --http <addr> --http-allow-host <name> --registry-root <dir>` (or the published container), the team's design imported into it once (an import into an empty store keeps the design's identity). The repo's `.mcp.json` (Claude Code) or Grok Build config lists `https://<name>/g/<id>/mcp`; a coworker opens the repo and their agent connects. Nothing to install, one place to upgrade, and everyone always on the same version.

WHAT IS CHEAP ABOUT IT: almost all of it is built. `--http`, `--http-allow-host` (cap:remote-sessions, verified) and the registry root serving `/g/<graph_id>/` are what flo2's droplet runs today. One process with many clients is one writer, so the single-writer store is fine. Sizing from flo2's droplet: 17 MB per process plus ~5 MB per open design, but CONCURRENT AGENT SESSIONS were observed at 0.5–1 GB each — size the instance by how many coworkers work at once. And the design stays on a company-controlled machine, which is a better home for work content than a personal service like flo2.

COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, RECORDED BESIDE IT:

🛑 1. "EXPOSE IT" IS THE PART THAT CANNOT BE DONE AS STATED. reflow2 authenticates nothing: `--http`'s own help says anything that can reach the port can write the design. On a public EC2 address that is the whole internet. Something in front has to decide who may reach it (dec:idea-authentication-is-somebody-elses-layer-and-the-line-is-the-contributor-id), cheapest first:
   · the company network only — a security group that admits the office or VPN range and nothing else. No code, no key; coworkers are on the VPN anyway. Cheapest by far.
   · a reverse proxy (Caddy, nginx, an AWS load balancer) with TLS that checks a shared team key sent as a header — both Claude Code's `.mcp.json` (`"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${TEAM_KEY}"}`) and Grok Build's `--header` can send one from an environment variable. Cheap.
   · the company's single sign-on in front (an OIDC proxy). The largest, and the only one that knows WHO each person is.

2. A SHARED KEY SAYS WHICH TEAM, NEVER WHICH PERSON. With a VPN or one team key, every coworker's write looks the same to reflow2. Credit per person needs each session to say who it writes for (the `writes_for` tool, v0.71.0) — taken on trust, fine among coworkers — or the SSO option passing identity through, which is what flo2 does. Settling intent (approving) stays the owner's word either way.

3. THE FILES — AND THIS IS THE REASON OPTION #2 EXISTS, so it is worth being plain about. Connected directly, the tools that touch files act on the EC2 instance's disk, not the coworker's: the design export lands on the server, not in the repo; registering and measuring a code file looks for it on the server. If the work repo commits `docs/design/*.json` and runs reflow2's design check in CI, that stops working, or someone has to bring the export back into the repo by hand. If the team keeps the design ONLY on the server and runs no design check in CI, none of this matters. The local client is not "running reflow2 locally": it is a small pass-through that makes the files land on the coworker's machine — but it IS an install, which is exactly what Alex wants to avoid. Zero install gives up the files; a small install keeps them.

4. IT RE-OPENS WHAT dec:central-host SETTLED. That decision (2026-08-26) chose option (c) — a hosted read/publish surface with WRITES KEPT LOCAL — over option (b), a hosted server that holds the writes. This idea is option (b) for a team. flo2 has since shown that hosted writes work in practice (api.flo2.io, with an authenticating gateway in front), so (b) deserves re-weighing — but it is a re-weighing, and should be taken as one.

5.
